Q: Runing sh or bash script cmds from the botton to the top A:

For a script with one command per line, reverse the lines and pipe them to the shell:

sh
tac script.sh | bash

cmd_n will be read first, then cmd_n-1, down to cmd_1. Use sh instead if the script is POSIX sh rather than Bash:

tac script.sh | sh

tac is the line-order reverse of cat; it outputs the file from last line to first line. Do not use rev for this, because rev reverses the characters inside each line, not the order of the lines.

This only works for simple scripts where each command is complete on one physical line. It will not correctly reverse shell syntax such as:

if condition; then
    cmd_1
fi

Reversing that line-by-line would put fi before if, which is not valid shell syntax. For scripts with functions, loops, if blocks, continuations with \, here-documents, or other multi-line constructs, there is no safe general “run the script backwards” transformation; write the reverse operations explicitly.

Q: Embedded systems interview A:

It's hard to answer this one because there are a wide variety of technical/coding interview styles. Every company seems to do it a little differently. I've had companies ask me to code something up on a whiteboard, I've had them ask me to complete a series of coding puzzles on an online platform, and I've even had companies that had their own in-house test software that was customized for their exact needs.

If you want practice, I recommend trying out a platform like Codewars, Codechef, LeetCode, etc. They have a large library of coding challenges that you can answer in a variety of languages. Set yourself a time limit and see how much you can do. Challenge yourself by seeing how many puzzles you can complete in an hour, or select a question and see how many different ways you can solve it, or how many languages you can solve it in. HackerRank even has a (paid) feature where you can do a mock coding interview with an AI.

When it comes to in-person interviews, understand that your answers really don't matter for the most part. Obviously, they want to weed out people that don't actually have the basic skills for the job. Beyond that, though, they're typically using coding as a way to answer more important questions like:

  • Would I actually want to work alongside this person? (in terms of work habits and personality)
  • Do they collaborate well with others, or are they a "lone wolf"?
  • Can they work independently, or do they need a lot of hand-holding?
  • Are they coachable?
  • Do they have the wisdom to anticipate problems and consequences?
  • Do they write code that's hard for someone else to understand and debug?

Personally, I have found the most effective approach to be doing everything out loud. Don't just explain your solution at the end, walk the interviewer through your entire thought process while you're having it. Ask questions any time there's any vagueness or missing information. Make it a conversation, even though you'll be doing 99% of the talking. If you can't talk to the interviewer and they're just watching your screen remotely while you type, then do the next best thing and write your comments first. Outline the entire program/function in prose, then go back and fill in the code. Document the decisions you made and why you made them. The end result is that the interviewer has a good idea of how you approach new situations and solve problems.

I think some of my best technical interview performances involved me writing the worst code. On one in particular, I was asked to take data that was structured in one format and convert it into another format. I started out writing something in C, with a few "<<insert X algorithm here>>" sections for algorithms I always forget under pressure. I got stuck at the end, asked a clarifying question, then proceeded to erase most of what I had written and tried a different approach. Within 15 minutes I had gone through probably 4 different implementations in 2 different languages, and then finally erased it all and did it in one sed command using the jankiest regular expression I've ever written. I got that job, by the way. After I was hired, I asked one of my coworkers who was in the interview about it. From my perspective, it was 15 minutes of failure culminating in an ugly solution that breaks when anything even remotely goes wrong. From his perspective, I could see a problem from multiple angles, I wasn't afraid to admit I was wrong, I was willing to find the best tool for the task instead of only using what I was most familiar with, and I didn't let frustration color the way I interacted with others. The only way he got that impression was because I was talking my way through the problem instead of just thinking silently and scribbling on a whiteboard. If you only saw my output, you'd think I'd lost my mind. Doing all my thinking out loud provided the insight needed for the interviewer to judge all the soft skills that they really cared about.

Q: Mutually referential arrays of structures A:

If you remove all decorations, the example would be a single line, that is valid in C and invalid in C++:

static int a[];
  • static int a[] is static int a[1] in C if it's not defined with a complete array type in the same translation unit (Clang compiler warns warning: array 'a' assumed to have one element)
  • static int a[] is invalid in C++ (error: storage size of 'a' isn't known)

BTW the last code snippet in the question is invalid and exhibits UB in C.

The answer to your main question

Why might the answers be different?

Because C and C++ are distinct programming languages.

Q: Injecting Blazor Web Assembly into existing project with .NET Core 6 A:

What you want already exits: the ASP.NET Core Hosted WASM template.

Add the ASP.NET Core Hosted WASM template to your current API project.

  • Update your project's Project file:
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.WebAssembly.Server" Version="7.0.4" />
  </ItemGroup>

  • Add Project dependencies to the Client and Shared projects to your project.

  • Update your project's Program

app.UseBlazorFrameworkFiles();
  • Sort out your default page/routing to what you want.
app.MapFallbackToFile("index.html");

Look at the server project's files for guidance.

Q: Script to check installed version doesnt execute all 'IF' commands A:

if is not limited to one command; every statement inside the { ... } block is part of that branch. If Write-Host "The version is outdated. Adding to list..." runs but the two Add-Content lines do not update C:\Logs\VMToolsVER.txt, the issue is with the file write or where the code is executing, not with the number of statements in the if block.

As posted, the second branch is also wrong syntax. else does not take a condition; use elseif for another test, as described in PowerShell's about_If help.

powershell
$logPath = 'C:\Logs\VMToolsVER.txt'

if ($currentVersion -lt $targetVersion) {
    Add-Content -Path $logPath -Value $Server -ErrorAction Stop
    Add-Content -Path $logPath -Value '' -ErrorAction Stop
    Write-Host 'The version is outdated. Adding to list...' -ForegroundColor Red
}
elseif ($currentVersion -eq $targetVersion) {
    Write-Host 'The exact target version is installed. No action needed.' -ForegroundColor Green
}

Check that C:\Logs exists and that the account running this code can write there. Add-Content can fail when the directory in the path does not exist, and -ErrorAction Stop makes that failure stop at the failing line instead of being missed in the surrounding script.

If the omitted full script uses Invoke-Command or another remoting mechanism, C:\Logs\VMToolsVER.txt is resolved on the remote computer running the script block. In that case, either check the file on the remote server or return $Server from the remote block and run Add-Content locally.
